rationale: Untranslated technical term in the pearl-formation chain: rain → ⲡⲝⲱⲃⲉ → oyster (ⲧⲃⲏⲧⲉ) → ⲡⲝⲉⲕ → ⲙⲁⲣⲅⲁⲣⲓⲧⲏⲥ (pearl). Possibly Lyc. dialectal term for nacre, coral-substance, or an intermediate gem-stage. Recurs lines 11, 28.

Earliest stage in the pearl-causation chain: 'the oyster also comes to be through the kobe.' Possibly Lyc. variant of ϫⲱⲃⲉ 'weak/small thing' or a sea-substrate term. Functions as the deep-water medium from which oysters arise.

Modifier of ⲛⲁⲟ̄ 'great' in 'great Iaos-gems' (lines 7, 20). Etymology unclear — possibly Greek-derived (ἴασις 'healing-stone'?) or an unidentified Lyc. gem-name. Functions in apposition with ⲙⲁⲣⲅⲁⲣⲓⲧⲏⲥ as a kind/class of pearl.
Compound on ⲡⲙⲟⲩⲛϩⲱⲩ 'downpour' (in glossary) with -ϩⲱⲗⲟ̄ likely incorporating the sweetness-root ϩⲗⲟϭ. Parallels the qualification of the drops as ⲉⲥϩⲁⲗⲟ̄ 'sweet' in line 2.
Conjunctive 3pl form 'and they sink in' from ϣⲱⲙⲥ 'submerge, dive' (cf. accumulated ⲁⲱⲙⲥ̄ for similar form). The drops sink into the oyster — standard motion-verb in pearl-formation parable.
Lyc. rendering of Greek κολυμβηταί 'divers,' with ⲝ for κ. Fits the parable's closing image: those who 'know it' (the pearl-bearing region) descend to those places and bring up myriads.

Recurring verb (lines 6, 15, 27) of pearls becoming great. Likely a Lyc. compound on a becoming-stem + ⲛⲁⲟ̄ 'great.' Functions as the verbal expression of the pearl's growth from a single drop into a great gem.
